docs.title: hsa-snoop
docs.text:
hsa-snoop traces AMD GPU workloads from user space, without touching the driver. It discovers AQL compute queues and SDMA copy queues via a dynamic kprobe, decodes every packet type including kernel dispatches and DMA copies, and emits Perfetto traces with queue-observed timing, kernel names, byte counts and directions.

sudo ./hsa-snoop -- ./my_hip_app     # launch + trace a single app
sudo ./hsa-snoop --all               # monitor every GPU process system-wide
# open traces at https://ui.perfetto.dev

docs.title: Tracked Performance
docs.text: Every hardware-test run on main records these counters. The performance tracker charts them per run, and the Prometheus snapshot lists every metric the latest run exported. Kernel timing records how long each test kernel takes.

docs.title: Where To Start
docs.text:
• Trace Queue Activity

    The usage guide covers every capture mode, the systemd unit and the dispatch log. Perfetto traces shows what the output looks like.

  • Export Live Metrics

    The Prometheus exporter publishes kernel launches, SDMA copies and AIS storage traffic during a capture, and the Grafana dashboard reads them.

  • Track Regressions

    The performance tracker charts the key counters from every CI run against an emulated GPU.

  • Understand The Internals

    How it works covers queue discovery, ring polling and SDMA decoding. See also the project layout and the limitations.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
cmake -B build
cmake --build build --parallel $(nproc)

Requires a C++17 compiler and CMake 3.21+. No third-party libraries. Add -DHSA_SNOOP_PROMETHEUS=ON for the Prometheus exporter. The repository covers testing and the HIP examples.

docs.title: Grafana Dashboard
docs.text:
Screenshot updated automatically by the grafana-screenshot CI workflow after each successful hardware-test run.

deploy/grafana/hsa-snoop-dashboard.json reads from two datasources:

  • Prometheus — Overview, Throughput, Duration, Queue, SDMA and AIS rows. Requires --prometheus.
  • Loki — Kernel Launch Timeline and hsa-snoop Logs rows. Requires --log-dispatches shipped into Loki via scripts/observability/.

The Prometheus rows work standalone; Loki rows stay empty without a log pipeline. Import the dashboard via Grafana's Dashboards → Import.

docs.title: Dashboard Development Workflow
docs.text:
Iterating on a dashboard means many minutes of clicking, and holding a --gres=gpu:1 Slurm allocation open for that is wasteful. The workflow is therefore capture-then-replay:

# 1. On a GPU node under Slurm: run a phased workload with the exporter and the
#    dispatch log on, then freeze a Prometheus TSDB snapshot plus the logs.
scripts/slurm/submit-obs.sh my-run

# 2. On the login node, with no allocation: replay them into a local
#    Grafana + Prometheus + Loki stack.
scripts/observability/stack.sh up results/my-run

# 3. Edit deploy/grafana/hsa-snoop-dashboard.json, then re-provision without
#    re-ingesting anything.
scripts/observability/stack.sh reload

# 4. Assert that every panel actually returns data.
scripts/observability/check-dashboard.py
scripts/observability/stack.sh down

check-dashboard.py walks the dashboard JSON, expands template and interval variables, and runs every target against the replayed datasources. This catches panels that are silently empty due to renamed labels or missing metrics.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
hsa-snoop has three stages, all in user space:

  1. Queue discovery — via the amdgpu/KFD driver. The ROCr runtime creates every AQL queue with the KFD create_queue ioctl (kfd_ioctl_create_queue). We install a dynamic ftrace kprobe on that function (by writing to /sys/kernel/tracing/kprobe_events) and read the struct kfd_ioctl_create_queue_args it was handed. That gives us, per queue: the ring base address, ring size, read/write pointers, GPU id and queue type. COMPUTE_AQL queues (type 2) are the host↔GPU AQL queues; SDMA (type 1) and SDMA_XGMI (type 3) are the DMA-copy queues. PM4 compute queues (type 0) are ignored.

The argument offsets come from the stable KFD uapi ABI (struct kfd_ioctl_create_queue_args), and the args pointer is the 3rd function argument (%dx on x86-64). No BTF or driver debuginfo is required.

A zero-build equivalent is provided for quick verification: sudo bpftrace scripts/hsa-snoop.bt.

  1. Physical address tracking. AQL ring buffers for host↔GPU communication live in host-accessible (GTT/system) memory. For each ring we resolve its physical address by walking /proc/<pid>/pagemap (needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN, i.e. run under sudo).

  2. Ring parsing — the activity snoop. The ring base and read/write pointers captured in step 1 are user virtual addresses in the target process (the KFD validates them as __user pointers). A per-queue poller reads them with process_vm_readv and watches write_dispatch_id vs read_dispatch_id:

  3. when the write id advances, the newly enqueued 64-byte AQL packet is decoded using the layouts in src/aql.h (mirrors <hsa/hsa.h>);
  4. when the read id passes a packet, it is marked queue-consumed.

Enqueue → queue-consumed host timestamps (CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW) give an approximate queue residency window for each dispatch. This is not the same as observing the packet completion signal or true GPU execution duration.

Kernel names are resolved from kernel_object (the runtime address of the kernel descriptor, i.e. the ELF *.kd symbol). We locate the AMDGPU (EM_AMDGPU) code-object ELFs in the process address space and walk their dynamic symbol tables. The descriptors the GPU actually uses live in device-backed (/dev/dri/renderD128) mappings, which process_vm_readv cannot read, so the resolver reads code objects through /proc/<pid>/mem instead. Names are demangled.

Output is written as a native Perfetto protobuf trace (default) or Chrome JSON (--format json); both open in https://ui.perfetto.dev.

docs.title: SDMA Capture
docs.text:
The same discovery kprobe also sees the SDMA (type 1) and SDMA_XGMI (type 3) queues — the GPU DMA copy engines. hipMemcpyAsync, peer-to-peer transfers and framework KV-cache staging are submitted here, not on the AQL compute queues, so they are invisible to hsa_kernel_launches_total. Capturing SDMA is the only user-space way to account for that bulk byte movement.

SDMA rings differ from AQL rings in three ways the parser handles separately (src/sdma.h, src/parser.cpp):

  • Variable-length packets. SDMA is dword-granular microcode, not fixed 64-byte slots. Each packet's header dword carries an 8-bit opcode + sub-opcode; the decoder reads the header, computes the length, decodes, then strides forward. Unknown opcodes trigger a resync rather than a bad stride.
  • The COPY packet carries the byte count and src/dst addresses. For linear copies we record bytes, src, dst and a direction.
  • Direction (H2D / D2H / D2D) is inferred by resolving the src/dst virtual addresses through /proc/<pid>/pagemap: a host page has a physical frame, a device (VRAM) page has none. src=host,dst=device → h2d, and so on. Results are cached per page.

Generation note. KFD/ROCR publish SDMA ring pointers as byte offsets; hsa-snoop normalises them to dword indices before walking packets. It detects the SDMA generation from the KFD gfx_target_version property and uses separate packet tables for CDNA SDMA v4.x (gfx9), RDNA3 SDMA v6.x (gfx11), and gfx12 SDMA v7.x (gfx1250 / MI455X). Unknown generations are ignored rather than decoded with the wrong layout. Use HSA_SNOOP_SDMA_DUMP=1 when calibrating a newly supported generation.

docs.title: Do We Need to Touch the Driver?
docs.text:
No. Everything is done by dynamically attaching to the running, stock out-of-tree amdgpu module:

  • queue discovery — dynamic ftrace kprobe on kfd_ioctl_create_queue (or the bundled bpftrace script). No source patch, no rebuild, no reload.
  • physical addresses — /proc/<pid>/pagemap.
  • ring contents & pointers — process_vm_readv / /proc/<pid>/mem.
  • kernel names — the process's own loaded code objects.

The KFD debugfs nodes (/sys/kernel/debug/kfd/mqds, hqds, rls) can be used as an independent cross-check of ring addresses but are not required.

A source-level tracepoint patch to amdgpu would only ever be needed if dynamic kprobe attach were unavailable (e.g. kfd_ioctl_create_queue inlined away); it is not needed on this platform (gfx90a, amdgpu 6.16 DKMS).

docs.title: Verifying the AQL Layouts
docs.text: src/aql.h is a self-contained copy of the packet formats so the tool builds without ROCm -dev headers. It is byte-compatible with /opt/rocm/include/hsa/hsa.h: static_asserts enforce the 64-byte packet size, and field offsets match hsa_kernel_dispatch_packet_t.

docs.text:

src/proc_mem.{h,cpp}               process_vm_readv + pagemap (VA->phys)

docs.title: hsa-snoop Limitations and Notes
docs.text:
• Sampling snoop, not a tap. Activity is captured by polling the ring. A packet that is enqueued and queue-consumed entirely within one poll interval can be missed (the slot may read back as INVALID once consumed). Lower --poll-us to catch faster kernels; deeply-queued workloads are captured near-completely (195/200 in the bundled test). Missed packets are exported as hsa_dispatches_missed_total in Prometheus mode, split by reason. The count covers every AQL packet type, so launches / (launches + missed) is a lower bound on the capture ratio for kernel dispatches.
  • GPU-timestamped durations need queue profiling in the workload. With GPU_FORCE_QUEUE_PROFILING=1 set for a HIP workload, the command processor stamps each dispatch, and hsa_kernel_gpu_duration_seconds reports those durations for every dispatch whose completion signal was read, however short the kernel. Three caveats. The stamps are in GPU clock ticks, whose rate is measured through KFD or given with --gpu-clock-hz; where neither is available the histogram stays empty. The runtime reuses a small pool of completion signals, so in a dense burst a dispatch can lose its stamps before they are read. And the interval starts when the command processor accepts the dispatch, so it can include time queued behind earlier kernels.
  • An idle queue is polled less often. A queue that has not moved for 10 ms is polled at a growing interval, up to --poll-idle-us (1000 by default). The first packets after an idle spell are therefore seen up to that much later, which can cost them their host-observed duration. --poll-idle-us 0 polls every queue at --poll-us always.
  • A read that blocks holds up a poll thread, and can cost a process its whole output. From ROCm 10.2 every read of a ring or of its pointers goes through the GPU driver (see below). When a GPU is out of memory such a read can block for a long time: with 24 processes on one emulated GPU, whose memory is full from about 16, single reads blocked for up to 96 s. Nothing is polled on that thread meanwhile, and hsa-snoop cannot put a time limit on a read. What was launched during the stall is decoded afterwards if the queue is still there and fewer packets than the ring holds have gone by, though without a duration. A process that exits during the stall takes its ring with it, and what it launched since its last poll is lost: it is in no missed counter, because the amount is not known. Three things limit this and make it visible:
    • --poll-threads <n> (default: the number of CPU cores, at most 4) polls with several threads. All queues of a process stay on one thread, so a blocked read holds up only the processes that share its thread, not every process. More threads cost more CPU while queues are busy; idle queues cost the same however many threads there are.
    • hsa_poller_stalled_seconds_total counts the time a poll thread was held up, and hsa_queues_unobserved_tail_total the queues that went away too long after their last successful poll for their end to have been seen. Both are described in the Prometheus page.
    • In every mode the same goes to the log: a [parser] poll thread ... stalled line (at most one per thread every 5 s), a [parser] queue ... went away ... after its last successful poll line per such queue, tail_unobserved=1 in that queue's [summary] line, and totals in the [summary] poller line at exit.

If these grow, run fewer processes per GPU or give the GPU more memory, and raise --poll-threads. Measured with 24 processes of 5,400 launches each on one emulated GPU, six runs for each setting: with one poll thread 75%, 79%, 79%, 79%, 99.7% and 99.9% of the launches were reported, with four threads 95.8%, 99.8%, 99.96% and three times 100%. More threads did not shorten the stalls, and at times several threads were held up together, so a process can still be lost. Every process that lost launches had tail_unobserved=1; so had most of those that lost none, because under this load most queues are last polled well before they go away. * Durations are sampled. hsa_kernel_duration_seconds is only observed for a packet the poller saw while it was still pending. A packet that was already consumed when first seen is counted as a launch but has no measurable duration, so on a workload of very short kernels the histogram count is well below hsa_kernel_launches_total. Those launches are counted in hsa_kernel_durations_unmeasured_total, so the sample rate is one minus unmeasured over launches (the query is in the Prometheus page); a lower --poll-us raises it at the cost of CPU. The sample is biased towards longer kernels, which are more likely to be seen pending. * Unresolved kernel names. A kernel whose descriptor cannot be matched to a symbol is labelled kernel_0x<addr>. The lookup is retried by up to three further scans of the process, at least 30 s apart, so a name that was unavailable at first sight is picked up for later launches under a new series. * Series without a pid label are never removed. The duration histograms and the --mem-snoop metrics have one series per kernel name and GPU, so they grow with the number of different kernel names seen, not with the number of processes. Kernels that stay unresolved are the exception: each kernel_0x<addr> label is a new name, and many short processes with unresolved kernels add series that stay. Series with a pid label are removed after --series-retain-sec; see the Prometheus page. * --mem-snoop reuses a snapshot of the process's VM map for up to one second, because reading /proc/<pid>/maps per dispatch stalls the poller on processes with thousands of mappings. A buffer mapped within the last second may be absent from mapped_vram for that dispatch. * Timing is host-observed. enqueue→queue-consumed uses host timestamps for queue pointer transitions, so a slice includes queue-wait time and may differ from true kernel execution or completion-signal timing. No profiling signals or counters are read; this is best used for structure and relative timing. * The startup scan stops each KFD process for an instant. In --pid and --all modes hsa-snoop attaches to every process that already has KFD queues, and has to stop its main thread briefly to let go of it again. A blocking system call that thread is in can return EINTR. Most programs retry; for a workload that does not, --no-scan skips the scan, at the price of not seeing queues that existed before hsa-snoop started. * Packets on a queue that already existed are reported from the first poll onwards. A queue seen being created by the KFD create_queue probe is decoded from the start of its ring. Queues found by the startup scan, and queues discovered through librocdxg on WSL2, start from the first poll. The [summary] line printed when a queue stops being polled gives the decoded and missed counts, how much was in the ring before the first poll, the number of successful polls, the longest time between two polls and whether the end of the queue went unobserved. * Attach mode only sees queues created after attach, since the kprobe fires on create_queue. Use launch mode to guarantee capture from process start. * AIS byte counts are the requested sizes of requests that succeeded. The return probe gives each request's status but not the bytes moved, so a short transfer is reported at its requested size. A failed request counts as an error and moves nothing. * hsa_kernel_duration_seconds is a coarse histogram by nature. Its buckets run 50 µs to 5 s on a 1-2.5-5 ladder, chosen against 96,749 measured dispatches so the fullest bucket holds ~42% of samples rather than the 72% the original decade ladder produced. histogram_quantile still interpolates inside a bucket, so a p99 is accurate to roughly the bucket width. When an exact percentile matters, take it from the --log-dispatches stream (quantile_over_time(... | unwrap dur_us ...)), which quantiles the individual measurements. The 50 µs floor is deliberate: durations come from polling the ring at --poll-us (default 20 µs), so anything below a couple of poll intervals is quantisation noise. * WSL2 PID mapping is heuristic. bpftrace reports host-kernel PIDs, which differ from WSL2 namespace PIDs by a fixed offset. In --all mode without a known target PID, hsa-snoop scans /proc by comm name to resolve the namespace PID. This can misattribute queues if two processes share the same comm prefix. Launch mode (-- <command>) avoids this by using the known child PID. * Physical addresses resolve for rings in ordinary process memory. A ring with no frame visible in pagemap reports ring_phys=0x0; that is also what a run without CAP_SYS_ADMIN sees. * From ROCm 10.2 every ring is a GPU buffer object. The runtime allocates AQL and SDMA rings as non-paged buffers mapped through the DRM render node, where 10.1 used anonymous memory. process_vm_readv cannot read such a mapping, so hsa-snoop reads it through /proc/<pid>/mem, which costs more per read. This applies to every GPU, and no runtime setting restores the old layout. The [queue] line shows what backs each ring as ring_backing=. * SDMA decode supports v4.x, v6.x, and v7.x packet layouts. v4 covers gfx9 CDNA (gfx90a / gfx942); v6 covers gfx11 RDNA3 (including gfx1101); v7 covers gfx12. Up to gfx12.4 the runtime writes the v6 packet set; from gfx12.5 (gfx1250 / MI455X) it writes variable-length copies with optional wait and signal blocks and 64-bit fence and poll packets, which are decoded as such. Unknown generations are ignored to avoid losing ring synchronisation. A packet the decoder does not recognise makes it skip to the write pointer; the [summary] line reports the skipped amount, which should be zero. Non-linear copy layouts (tiled, sub-window) and copies to several destinations are counted and stepped over but do not yet contribute a byte total. * SDMA copy direction is a pagemap heuristic. A src/dst page with no PFN is treated as device (VRAM) memory; this also matches a not-present/swapped host page, so a copy touching a paged-out host buffer can be misclassified. For live, pinned copy buffers (the common case) it is accurate. * Verified on: gfx90a (MI2xx / Aldebaran), ROCm 7.1.0, amdgpu 6.16 DKMS, kernel 6.8, x86-64; gfx1101 SDMA v6 COPY_LINEAR; gfx1250 (MI455X) SDMA v7 COPY_LINEAR via rocjitsu/vfio-user. SDMA capture calibration is in progress on gfx942 (MI3xx).

docs.title: Perfetto Trace Visualization
docs.text:
hsa-snoop emits native Perfetto traces that can be opened in Perfetto UI. Each AQL or SDMA queue gets its own timeline track; selecting a slice exposes decoded metadata including grid dimensions, kernel object, segment sizes and completion signals.

Full trace showing packet activity across two AQL queues Kernel dispatches and barrier packets, with decoded dispatch metadata

Note: hsa-snoop slices represent approximate enqueue-to-queue-consumed residency, not GPU execution time.

Output format is native Perfetto protobuf (.pftrace, default) or Chrome JSON (--format json); both open in https://ui.perfetto.dev.

docs.title: Prometheus Exporter
docs.text:
Requires -DHSA_SNOOP_PROMETHEUS=ON at build time.

sudo ./hsa-snoop --all --prometheus                  # serve on default port 9488
sudo ./hsa-snoop --all --prometheus-port 9100        # custom port
curl http://localhost:9488/metrics

docs.title: HSA / GPU Metrics
docs.text:
All metrics carry constant labels host, platform, rocm_version, discovery_mode.

Options that shape the labels and the series:

Option Environment Effect --host-label <s> HSA_SNOOP_HOST_LABEL Value of host. Defaults to the host name, which in a container is the container id and changes on every recreate; set it to the node name there. --rocm-version <s> HSA_SNOOP_ROCM_VERSION Value of rocm_version. Defaults to the version found under /opt/rocm, or unknown when ROCm is installed only in the traced containers. --gpu-clock-hz <hz> HSA_SNOOP_GPU_CLOCK_HZ GPU clock rate used for hsa_kernel_gpu_duration_seconds. Defaults to a rate measured through KFD. --kernel-name-max <n> — Truncate kernel_name values to n bytes (ending in ...). Default 0, no limit. Names that differ only past the cut share one series. --poll-threads <n> — Number of ring poll threads, 1 to 64. Default: the number of CPU cores, at most 4. All queues of a process are polled by one thread. See Poller health. --series-retain-sec <n> HSA_SNOOP_SERIES_RETAIN_SEC How long the series of a process outlive its last queue. Default 300; 0 keeps them for ever. See Series lifecycle.

hsa_kernel_duration_seconds is sampled. hsa_kernel_launches_total carries kernel_name and the unmeasured counter does not, so aggregate both sides to get the sample rate:

1 - sum by (gpu_id, pid, comm) (rate(hsa_kernel_durations_unmeasured_total[5m]))
  / sum by (gpu_id, pid, comm) (rate(hsa_kernel_launches_total[5m]))
Metric Type Labels Description hsa_snoop_up Gauge — 1 when the exporter is running hsa_kernel_launches_total Counter kernel_name, gpu_id, gpu_type, pid, comm Kernel dispatch count. Vendor packets that are not kernel launches are not counted hsa_kernel_duration_seconds Histogram kernel_name, gpu_id, gpu_type Kernel duration (host-observed, enqueue to queue-consumed) hsa_kernel_gpu_duration_seconds Histogram kernel_name, gpu_id, gpu_type Kernel duration from the command processor's own timestamps. Only for workloads run with queue profiling on (GPU_FORCE_QUEUE_PROFILING=1 for HIP) hsa_gpu_clock_ticks_per_second Gauge gpu_id, gpu_type GPU clock rate used for that conversion hsa_kernel_durations_unmeasured_total Counter gpu_id, gpu_type, pid, comm Launches with no duration observation (see the sample-rate query below) hsa_kernel_launches_per_second Gauge gpu_id, gpu_type Rolling 10 s launch rate hsa_last_kernel_launch_timestamp_seconds Gauge gpu_id, gpu_type Wall-clock time of most recent launch hsa_last_kernel_launch_info Gauge gpu_id, gpu_type, kernel_name Most recently launched kernel name (value always 1) hsa_active_queues Gauge gpu_id, gpu_type AQL queues being polled now. Goes down when a queue is destroyed or its process exits hsa_queue_info Gauge gpu_id, gpu_type, pid, comm, ring_base, ring_phys, ring_size One series per queue being polled now (value always 1). Removed as soon as the queue is dropped hsa_barrier_packets_total Counter gpu_id, gpu_type, pid, comm Barrier AQL packets seen hsa_sdma_copies_total Counter gpu_id, gpu_type, pid, comm, direction SDMA copy packets, by direction (h2d/d2h/d2d) hsa_sdma_bytes_total Counter gpu_id, gpu_type, pid, comm, direction Bytes moved by SDMA copies hsa_sdma_packets_total Counter gpu_id, gpu_type, pid, comm, opcode SDMA packets by opcode hsa_active_sdma_queues Gauge gpu_id, gpu_type SDMA queues being polled now hsa_sdma_present Gauge — 1 when first SDMA queue seen; 0 on APU/unified-memory nodes hsa_triggered Gauge gpu_id, gpu_type 1 on first kernel dispatch on this GPU hsa_errors_total Counter gpu_id, pid Packets before queue registration hsa_dispatches_missed_total Counter gpu_id, gpu_type, pid, comm, reason AQL packets not decoded. reason is overwritten (the ring wrapped before they were read), consumed (already consumed and the slot no longer holds a packet that can be decoded) or unreadable (the slot read failed). Counts every packet type, not only kernel dispatches hsa_poller_stalled_seconds_total Counter thread Time a poll thread was held up with queues overdue for a poll. See Poller health hsa_queues_unobserved_tail_total Counter gpu_id, gpu_type, kind Queues (kind is aql or sdma) that went away too long after their last successful poll, or without ever being read. What they did in that time is in no other counter hsa_xnack_total Counter pasid, comm GPU page-fault retries (--xnack-snoop)

Per-GPU totals of the per-process counters above. They count the same events across all processes and are never removed:

Metric Labels Total of hsa_gpu_kernel_launches_total gpu_id, gpu_type hsa_kernel_launches_total hsa_gpu_kernel_durations_unmeasured_total gpu_id, gpu_type hsa_kernel_durations_unmeasured_total hsa_gpu_dispatches_missed_total gpu_id, gpu_type, reason hsa_dispatches_missed_total hsa_gpu_barrier_packets_total gpu_id, gpu_type hsa_barrier_packets_total hsa_gpu_sdma_copies_total gpu_id, gpu_type, direction hsa_sdma_copies_total hsa_gpu_sdma_bytes_total gpu_id, gpu_type, direction hsa_sdma_bytes_total hsa_gpu_sdma_packets_total gpu_id, gpu_type, opcode hsa_sdma_packets_total

docs.title: Series lifecycle
docs.text:
Every series with a pid label belongs to one process. When the last queue of that process is gone (it exited, or shut its runtime down), its series are kept for --series-retain-sec seconds, 300 by default, and then removed from /metrics. Without this a node where jobs come and go would export a few more series for every process it has ever seen, and hsa-snoop's memory would grow with them.

  • Set the retention to at least two scrape intervals. A series has to be scraped once after its last change for Prometheus to hold its final value.
  • The retention starts over if the process comes back. A new queue of the same pid inside the period keeps the series and their counts. After the period a reused pid starts new series from 0, which rate() and increase() handle as a counter reset.
  • hsa_queue_info is not retained. It is removed with its queue, so a queue that lives for less than a scrape interval may never be scraped. The queue events of --log-dispatches record every queue.
  • AIS operation counts (ais_rx_ops_total, ais_tx_ops_total) carry a pid too. For a process with no queue (one outside --pid, or a thread other than the main one, which AIS reports under its own id) they are kept for as long as the process or thread exists, however long it goes between two operations, and removed the retention period after it is found gone.
  • --series-retain-sec 0 keeps every series for as long as hsa-snoop runs, as releases up to 1.9.0 did. The two active-queue gauges and hsa_queue_info follow the live queues all the same.

What this means for counters: a per-process counter is not monotonic for the life of hsa-snoop, because it disappears. Summing it over processes, as in sum by (gpu_id) (hsa_kernel_launches_total), gives a value that drops each time a process's series are removed. sum(rate(...)) and sum(increase(...)) are not affected, since Prometheus computes them per series before summing. For a total that only ever goes up, use the hsa_gpu_*_total counters. The histograms, the per-GPU gauges and the --mem-snoop metrics have no pid label and are never removed.

docs.title: Poller health
docs.text:
hsa-snoop sees a queue only when it polls it. Two counters say when it could not, so that a gap in the other metrics is not mistaken for a quiet GPU. Neither has a pid label and neither is ever removed.

  • hsa_poller_stalled_seconds_total has one series per poll thread (--poll-threads). It grows by the time a thread got to a queue later than the queue was due, once that is more than 50 ms (or more than the queue's own interval, for an idle queue polled less often than that). Time during which several queues of a thread were overdue is counted once. A thread is normally held up by a read of a process's memory that blocks in the kernel, which happens when a GPU is out of memory; none of that thread's queues is looked at meanwhile. If the queue being read goes away during such a read, the time the thread was held in it is counted as well, even when the thread has no other queue left. Launches made during a stall are still decoded afterwards as long as the queue is still there and its ring has not wrapped, but their durations are wrong or unmeasured.
  • hsa_queues_unobserved_tail_total counts queues whose end was not seen: the queue went away more than about 50 ms after its last successful poll (more for an idle queue with a longer poll interval), or was never read at all. The time is taken up to the read that failed, so what hsa-snoop then spends finding out why is not held against the queue. Whatever the queue did in that time is lost, and no missed counter includes it, because the amount is not known. A process usually has two or three queues, and each counts.

Both say where to distrust the other numbers, not how much is missing: a queue counted here may have done nothing in the time it was not watched. In the overload test described in the limitations page every process that lost launches had a queue counted here, and so did most that lost none. Both stay at 0 on a system that is keeping up, so alert on any increase of the second and on a sustained rate of the first:

increase(hsa_queues_unobserved_tail_total[10m]) > 0
sum(rate(hsa_poller_stalled_seconds_total[5m])) > 0.05

What to do when they grow: run fewer processes per GPU or give the GPU more memory, so that reads stop blocking; and raise --poll-threads, so that one blocked read holds up fewer processes. See the limitations page for what was measured.

docs.title: AIS Metrics
docs.text:
All require --ais-snoop. Labels: gpu_id, gpu_type, pcie_id, device_type, vendor.

Metric Type Description ais_snoop_armed Gauge 1 if AIS kprobe started; absent if --ais-snoop not passed ais_active Gauge 1 on first AIS operation ais_rx_ops_total / ais_tx_ops_total Counter AIS ioctls completed ais_rx_bytes_total / ais_tx_bytes_total Counter P2P DMA bytes transferred ais_rx_errors_total / ais_tx_errors_total Counter Failed operations (extra errno label) ais_rx_latency_seconds / ais_tx_latency_seconds Histogram ioctl entry-to-return latency ais_rx_io_size_bytes / ais_tx_io_size_bytes Histogram Requested transfer size ais_pcie_device_info Gauge Info metric per PCIe device

docs.title: WSL2 / librocdxg Mode
docs.text:
On Windows Subsystem for Linux 2, the amdgpu KFD device is not present. Instead, AMD's librocdxg library bridges HSA calls through the Windows DXG kernel interface. hsa-snoop detects WSL2 automatically and switches to bpftrace mode:

sudo ./hsa-snoop -- ./my_hip_app     # auto-selects bpftrace on WSL2

Or force it explicitly on any system:

sudo ./hsa-snoop --mode bpftrace -- ./my_hip_app
sudo ./hsa-snoop --mode bpftrace --all

In bpftrace mode, hsa-snoop forks a bpftrace child that attaches a uprobe to hsaKmtCreateQueueExt in librocdxg.so. The library path is auto-detected via /opt/rocm/lib/librocdxg.so; pass --librocdxg <path> to override. bpftrace must be installed and the process must run as root.

docs.title: Startup Scan for Pre-existing Queues
docs.text:
hsa-snoop automatically scans all running KFD processes at startup using the KFD debug-trap API (AMDKFD_IOC_DBG_TRAP / KFD_IOC_DBG_TRAP_GET_QUEUE_SNAPSHOT). This discovers queues that were created before hsa-snoop started, with full metadata (ring VA, wptr, rptr, gpu_id, queue type). The scan runs in launch mode is skipped (the target process hasn't started yet); in --pid and --all modes it runs automatically before the event-driven probe is armed.

The scan attaches to each target process with PTRACE_SEIZE and briefly enables KFD debug mode on it (milliseconds), because the driver only answers the queue snapshot for a process's tracer. The process keeps running while it is queried. To let go of it again hsa-snoop has to stop it for an instant, since the kernel only detaches a stopped process; once the scan has finished, TracerPid in /proc/<pid>/status is back to 0 and the process can be debugged, signalled and reaped as usual. A process that is already being traced, by a debugger for instance, cannot be attached and is skipped. The scan requires CAP_SYS_PTRACE (root), which hsa-snoop already requires. KFD ioctl minor version ≥ 1.13 is required (Linux ~6.1 / AMDGPU ~5.7).

That instant has one side effect. It is the main thread of the process that is stopped, and if that thread is blocked in a system call the kernel does not restart on its own (epoll_wait, semop, msgrcv, a socket read with a receive timeout, among others), the call returns EINTR although no signal was delivered. Python and most event-loop libraries retry such calls. For a workload that treats EINTR as an error, start hsa-snoop with --no-scan: nothing is attached or stopped, and only queues created after hsa-snoop started are traced.

docs.title: Trace Files in --all Mode
docs.text: In --all mode without --prometheus, hsa-snoop keeps one trace per queue and writes it to --out-dir (default /var/log/hsa-snoop) when the queue goes away, that is when its process exits or destroys it. Traces of queues that are still live are written when hsa-snoop exits. Each file is named <command>-<uid>.pftrace (or .json), where <command> is the name of the process that owns the queue and <uid> is the queue uid shown in the [queue] log lines, for example gfx-test-3.json. The name is announced when the queue is found (new trace → ...) and again when the file is written. Characters in the process name other than letters, digits, ., _, - and + are replaced with _.

docs.title: Probes Left by a Killed hsa-snoop
docs.text: hsa-snoop removes its kprobes when it exits, including on SIGINT and SIGTERM. One that is killed with SIGKILL cannot, and its probes (hsasnoop_cq_<pid>, and with --ais-snoop also hsasnoop_ais_e_<pid>, hsasnoop_ais_r_<pid> and the tracefs instance hsa_ais_<pid>) stay installed. The next hsa-snoop to start removes every such probe whose <pid> is no longer a running hsa-snoop, and logs each removal. Probes that belong to an hsa-snoop that is still running are left alone.

docs.title: Poll Threads (--poll-threads)
docs.text:
The rings are polled by several threads: as many as there are CPU cores, up to 4, unless --poll-threads <n> (1 to 64) says otherwise. A queue is assigned by the pid of its process, so all queues of one process are polled by the same thread and its records keep their order. Records of different processes can reach the dispatch log in a different order than they were submitted in; each line carries its own timestamp.

The point of more than one thread is isolation. A read of a process's memory can block in the GPU driver when the GPU is out of memory, and nothing else is polled on that thread until it returns. With one thread that is every process; with four it is a quarter of them. Each thread polls at --poll-us while any of its queues is busy, so CPU use under load grows with the number of threads in use. Idle queues do not cost more with more threads: a thread with no queues sleeps, and so does one whose queues are all idle, while one extra thread looks at the idle queues of all of them every --poll-idle-us and wakes the owner of any that moves. That extra thread is shared, so it is supervised by a timer: if a read blocks it and it has not come round for a few idle intervals, every poll thread goes back to polling its own idle queues until the read returns.

--poll-threads 1 is the behaviour of releases up to 1.9.0. When a poll thread is held up, hsa-snoop says so in its log and, in Prometheus mode, in hsa_poller_stalled_seconds_total and hsa_queues_unobserved_tail_total; see "Poller health" in the Prometheus page.

docs.title: Dispatch Event Log (--log-dispatches)
docs.text:
Prometheus is an aggregating store sampled at the scrape interval. At the ~2700 kernel launches/s a tight HIP loop reaches, a 1 s scrape collapses thousands of distinct dispatches into a single counter delta, and no dashboard built on it can show which kernel ran when. --log-dispatches is the other half: one NDJSON line per event, with a wall-clock RFC3339 timestamp, written independently of both the trace files and the exporter.

sudo ./hsa-snoop --all --prometheus --log-dispatches /var/log/hsa-snoop/events.ndjson
sudo ./hsa-snoop -- ./my_hip_app --log-dispatches -      # '-' means stderr

{"ts":"2026-09-01T22:04:28.106365Z","ev":"queue","kind":"aql","gpu_id":10976,"pid":1795691,"comm":"gfx-test","queue_uid":1,"qtype":2,"ring_size":4096,"ring_va":"0x7097172a9000","ring_phys":"0x63f49cc000"}
{"ts":"2026-09-01T22:04:28.392511Z","ev":"dispatch","gpu_id":10976,"pid":1795691,"comm":"gfx-test","queue_uid":2,"dispatch_id":0,"kernel":"vadd(float const*, float const*, float*, int)","grid":[26624,1,1],"wg":[256,1,1],"lds":0,"scratch":0,"dur_us":812.500}

ev is one of queue, dispatch or sdma. dur_us is present only when the queue was observed to retire the packet; 64-bit addresses are hex strings, because JSON numbers are IEEE doubles in most consumers and would silently lose the low bits. Available in every build — it does not require -DHSA_SNOOP_PROMETHEUS=ON.

This is the stream the Grafana kernel-launch timeline is built from; ship it into Loki with the Alloy config under scripts/observability/.

[!NOTE] The log is written unbuffered-per-line from the parser sink thread. At a sustained few thousand dispatches/s it produces on the order of 15 MB/minute, so point it at local storage rather than NFS for long runs.

docs.title: Quick Discovery-Only Check (No Build)
docs.text: sudo bpftrace scripts/hsa-snoop.bt

docs.title: Running as a systemd Daemon
docs.text:
Requires a build with -DHSA_SNOOP_PROMETHEUS=ON.

# Configure with the same install prefix you intend to deploy.
cmake -B build -DHSA_SNOOP_PROMETHEUS=ON -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=/usr/local
cmake --build build --parallel

# Install binary and unit files to the prefix chosen above
sudo cmake --install build

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now hsa-snoop-prometheus

# Check status / live logs
sudo systemctl status hsa-snoop-prometheus
sudo journalctl -fu hsa-snoop-prometheus

# Verify the metrics endpoint
curl http://localhost:9488/metrics

The packaged/systemd-managed daemon is hsa-snoop-prometheus.service. Prometheus-enabled installs also stage /etc/default/hsa-snoop; edit it to tune the daemon (poll interval, optional snoops, etc.), then run sudo systemctl restart hsa-snoop-prometheus.service.

To change the port, set it in HSA_SNOOP_ARGS or override ExecStart in a drop-in:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/hsa-snoop-prometheus.service.d
cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/hsa-snoop-prometheus.service.d/port.conf
[Service]
ExecStart=
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/hsa-snoop --all --prometheus --prometheus-port 9100
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart hsa-snoop-prometheus

docs.title: Grafana Dashboard Development
docs.text:
Iterating on a dashboard means many minutes of clicking, and holding a --gres=gpu:1 Slurm allocation open for that is wasteful. The workflow is therefore capture-then-replay:

# 1. On a GPU node under Slurm: run a phased workload with the exporter and the
#    dispatch log on, then freeze a Prometheus TSDB snapshot plus the logs.
scripts/slurm/submit-obs.sh my-run

# 2. On the login node, with no allocation: replay them into a local
#    Grafana + Prometheus + Loki stack.
scripts/observability/stack.sh up results/my-run

# 3. Edit deploy/grafana/hsa-snoop-dashboard.json, then re-provision without
#    re-ingesting anything.
scripts/observability/stack.sh reload

# 4. Assert that every panel actually returns data.
scripts/observability/check-dashboard.py
scripts/observability/stack.sh down

check-dashboard.py walks the dashboard JSON, expands Grafana's template and interval variables, and runs every target against the replayed datasources. Loading a dashboard in a browser tells you it renders; this tells you which panels are silently empty because a label was renamed or a metric is only created after the first error.

docs.title: Performance Tracker
docs.text:
Each point is one hardware-test run on main: a fixed workload against an emulated GPU, traced with hsa-snoop --prometheus. The values are counter totals for that workload, so a change means the tool observed more or less activity than it did before, not that anything ran faster.

docs.title: Where The Numbers Come From
docs.text:
The vm-hardware-test workflow scrapes the exporter at the end of its run and hands the exposition text to .github/ci/report/publish-perf.py, which appends one record to perf/history.jsonl on the gh-pages branch and refreshes the perf/badge-*.json files behind the README badges. Nothing in main carries performance data; this page fetches the history when it loads.

The same run publishes every metric it exported, not only the four tracked here, to the Prometheus snapshot. Per-kernel durations from that run are on the kernel timing page.

docs.title: Prometheus Snapshot
docs.text:
Every metric exported by the most recent successful hardware-test run on main, collected from the test VM via hsa-snoop --prometheus and grouped by metric family. The Prometheus exporter page documents what each one means; the performance tracker charts four of them over time.

docs.title: Kernel Timing
docs.text:
Per-kernel timing for the gfx-test HIP kernels (vadd, vscale, vdot), captured by every hardware-test run on main against an emulated gfx1250 GPU. Helper kernels from the HIP runtime appear too.

Two durations are recorded for each dispatch, and they are not the same measurement:

GPU ticks

The interval between the start and end timestamps the GPU command processor writes into the dispatch's completion signal. Present only when the workload runs with profiling enabled, described below. These are raw GPU clock ticks, not a time. The start is when the command processor accepted the dispatch, so kernels launched back to back overlap and the later ones include time spent waiting.

Queue µs

The time from when hsa-snoop first saw the packet on the ring to when it saw the dispatch finish, by polling. Always present, and no finer than the poll interval. A dispatch with a completion signal finishes when the signal fires; one without is counted as finished when the command processor takes it off the queue, which is earlier.

The GPU here is emulated, so neither number says how fast real hardware runs these kernels. What the page tracks is whether they move from one commit to the next.

Loading the published history…

docs.text: Median per kernel, one point per run.

docs.title: Enabling GPU Timestamps
docs.text:
Two things have to be true for a dispatch to carry timestamps.

Profiling must be enabled on the queue. libhsa-snoop-profiler.so does this: it is an HSA_TOOLS_LIB plugin that the HSA runtime loads at start-up, and it enables profiling on every compute queue the workload creates.

The dispatch must have a completion signal, because that is where the command processor writes the timestamps. HIP only attaches one to a kernel launch when command profiling is on, so set GPU_FORCE_QUEUE_PROFILING=1 as well.

sudo env HSA_TOOLS_LIB=$PWD/build/libhsa-snoop-profiler.so \
  GPU_FORCE_QUEUE_PROFILING=1 \
  ./build/hsa-snoop --log-dispatches dispatches.ndjson -- ./my_hip_app

hsa-snoop reads the timestamps out of the signal when it fires, and --log-dispatches writes them as gpu_start_ticks and gpu_end_ticks.

docs.title: Where The Numbers Come From
docs.text: The vm-hardware-test workflow runs .github/ci/report/capture-kernel-timing.sh in the test VM after the hardware tests pass, and fails the run if the shim does not load, no dispatch resolves to a kernel name, or none carries GPU timestamps. .github/ci/report/publish-kernel-timing.py then summarises the dispatch log per kernel, appends one record to timing/history.jsonl on the gh-pages branch and refreshes the badge. Pull requests get the same table in the workflow run summary, without publishing.
